extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in media studies, computational social science, and climate communication (authors doing large-scale content analysis of news coverage)
extracted.subtask_description: Automated content analysis (topic modeling) of U.S. newspaper articles about climate change across 1997–2017 to detect thematic prevalence and outlet-level biases by partisan orientation, scale, and local climate vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus selection (sources and diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data was collected from full-text articles available in 52 newspapers indexed across the LexisNexis, Newspaper Source Plus, and U.S. Newsstream databases. The selected newspapers are diverse in terms of geography, partisan orientation, and scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large commercial news databases to assemble a diverse set of outlets (national, large regional, small regional) to avoid outlet bias toward prestige press; map newspapers geographically and note availability limits for some outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles were collected from the years 1997–2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a multi-year span (here two decades) to capture temporal variation and major events influencing coverage; report any newspapers with limited year coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article retrieval & initial de-duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: A Boolean search for “climate change” or “global warming” in the 52 newspapers returned 176,982 unique articles after removing duplicate entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document query terms, search scope, and the process for removing duplicate entries before further filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article inclusion threshold (focus filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: To restrict the corpus to newspaper articles primarily focused on climate change, articles were filtered by whether they made at least two mentions of the phrases “climate change,” “global warming,” or “greenhouse gas.” This left 78,599 articles for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a clear mention-count threshold (here >=2) to exclude incidental mentions and produce a corpus concentrated on the topic of interest; report the resulting corpus size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text inclusion/exclusion (visual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text from figure captions are included in the data, but not text embedded in an image such as an infographic. Data regarding the inclusion of visual content in an article was not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state what parts of articles were parsed (body text, captions) and what was excluded (embedded image text), as visual content may be unavailable from databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan orientation measurement (editorial endorsements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partisan orientation was measured by presidential endorsements from newspaper editorial boards since 1996 (+1 for Democratic candidate endorsements, −1 for Republican candidate endorsements, and 0 for no endorsement). Scores < −2 labeled 'conservative' (16 papers), −2 to 2 'moderate' (18), >2 'liberal' (18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial-board presidential endorsements as a proxy for outlet political leaning, report coding scheme and thresholds, and note caveat that reporters may not share editorial board orientation; cite source of endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of circulation categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper scale was categorized as 'national' (six named papers), 'large regional' (23 papers with circulations >100,000 in 2015), and 'small regional' (24 papers). Circulation data were collected from Alliance for Audited Media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define scale categories and threshold values (e.g., >100,000), list which outlets fall into each category, and cite circulation data source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate vulnerability measurement (ND-GAIN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulnerability was measured using ND-GAIN Urban Adaptation Assessment overall climate risk. Newspapers in areas >=1 standard deviation above mean labeled 'High' (12), <=1 standard deviation below mean 'Low' (6), others 'Medium' (34). Alternative operational definitions (above vs below mean) were also explored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an established vulnerability index, specify cutoffs (±1 SD), report counts per category, and test alternative operationalizations for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text preprocessing steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard data preprocessing: reduce words to word stems, remove punctuation, numbers, and common stop words. Words that occurred fewer than 25 times or in more than 90% of documents were also removed. Compound phrases (e.g., 'climate change') were identified using textstat_collocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document stemming, stop word removal, punctuation/number removal, lower/upper frequency thresholds (min frequency = 25, max prevalence = 90%), and detection/representation of multiword expressions before building term-document matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-document matrix construction and feature engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: After preprocessing, build the term-document matrix from which topic models are estimated, including compound phrase handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe feature construction choices (stemming vs lemmatization, collocations), and the thresholds applied which affect vocabulary size and topic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic modeling method and software
rubrics_metrics.description: A dynamic topic model was estimated using the stm R package (Roberts et al., 2014a). Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)-style topic modeling principles were used to infer k latent topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the model family (dynamic/topic model/STM), software package and version, and theoretical basis (LDA/STM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection guidance (number of topics k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generality scores representing topic exclusivity and semantic coherence were inspected to guide selection of number of topics; after inspecting several candidates, a model with 28 topics was selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute model diagnostics (e.g., generality, coherence, exclusivity) across candidate k values, visualize metrics (Appendix A), and choose k based on combined quantitative diagnostics and substantive interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic labeling (FREX + qualitative inspection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic labels were determined through interpretation of associated word stems that were frequent and exclusive to each topic (FREX scoring) as well as a qualitative inspection of the 25 most representative newspaper articles for each topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine FREX or other combined-frequency-and-exclusivity scores with human inspection of representative documents (e.g., top 25) to assign meaningful labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: External validity checks (temporal/event correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach to validating topics is whether their temporal patterns conform to external events (e.g., Religion topic spiked in 2015 with Laudato Si’, International Agreements spiked when Kyoto Protocol debates were prominent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare topic prevalence over time to known events; use spikes and expected temporal patterns as evidence of external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human validation: word intrusion and topic intrusion tests
rubrics_metrics.description: External validation assessed via word intrusion and topic intrusion tests. Word intrusion: 12 reviewers saw five probable words plus an intruder; Topic intrusion: 8 reviewers read an article and were presented with the high-scoring topic plus two low-scoring topics. Report percent agreement identifying intrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run word and topic intrusion tests with multiple human reviewers, report agreement rates per topic (percentage correct), and identify topics with lower external validity (e.g., 'Campaigns' and 'Letters to the Editor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-document inspection for substantive interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative inspection of the most representative articles for each topic was used both to label topics and to interpret whether high-scoring documents contained refutations or endorsements of frames (e.g., Climate Change Denial topic included both denial arguments and refutations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect representative documents to understand topic composition, whether topics mix contesting frames, and to inform interpretation of partisan differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of topic prevalence comparisons across outlet attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare topic prevalence over time by outlet attributes (partisan orientation, scale, climate vulnerability) to detect systematic differences in coverage (e.g., conservative outlets covered Climategate more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratify topic prevalence by outlet metadata and visualize temporal patterns to identify where and when outlet bias appears; interpret patterns in light of geography and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of event-driven spikes and thematic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spikes in topic prevalence to strategically read documents at specific points in time and identify meaningful content driving topics (e.g., Climategate, IPCC reports, Hurricanes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage temporal visualizations of topics to locate key events, then examine representative articles within spikes to validate topic meaning and causal drivers of attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and limitations documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations such as database coverage not being exhaustive, some newspapers having limited availability across years, inability to capture embedded image text, and that editorial-board endorsements are a proxy for audience orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list dataset and measurement limitations, examine alternative operationalizations (e.g., vulnerability above vs below mean), and caution about over-interpretation of topic content (mixed articles etc.).
